Judgement Is the Moat

By lowob · 31 August 2026 · Updated 9 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Strategy / AI & Marketing

A team can now produce a month's worth of posts, landing-page drafts and campaign ideas in an afternoon. That sounds like progress. But if nobody has decided who the work is for or what it needs to accomplish, faster production doesn't solve much.

This is a useful distinction for companies buying AI marketing tools or hiring people to use them. Producing the material is getting easier. Knowing what is worth publishing remains difficult.

More output isn't the same as better marketing

AI can turn a founder interview into a blog post, a newsletter, a series of social updates and a set of sales messages. It can summarize competitors, suggest headlines and help a small team do work that previously required several specialists. Those are real advantages.

But they only help when the underlying idea is worth communicating. In Ahrefs' September 2026 survey of 301 marketers, 93% said they were using AI to create or help create content. The same survey found 69% were publishing more AI-assisted content than a year earlier. This is a survey of respondents, not proof that the additional content made those businesses more successful.

When so many teams can produce the same kinds of material, the number of articles or social posts published is a poor measure of whether the marketing is doing its job.

What judgement looks like in an actual project

Imagine a DeFi app whose website attracts visitors but whose wallet-connection numbers barely move. An AI assistant can suggest dozens of campaigns about the product's yield, its security and the size of the market. It cannot settle the basic question on its own: are people confused by the message, or is the product itself difficult to use?

The first useful move is to look at the experience. Where do visitors leave? Can they tell what happens after connecting a wallet? Do the people the company hopes to reach actually trust the product? If the problem is an unclear deposit process, commissioning more promotional content is unlikely to fix it.

This example is hypothetical, but the distinction is practical. Choosing the next piece of content depends on knowing what is stopping customers, not just on having a tool capable of writing it.

Good marketing judgement is often a sequence of ordinary decisions: choose one audience, understand what it needs to believe, test whether your claims are supportable, and decide which work deserves time or money. The final output comes after that thinking, not instead of it.

Give AI a clear job, and keep people responsible for the decisions

AI is most useful when a team can tell whether its work is right. Ask it to organize interview notes, compare drafts against approved product facts, summarize objections from sales calls, or prepare variants of a message the team has already decided to test. Those tasks are easier to review because the underlying information is available.

It is less sensible to let a polished draft quietly become the company's position. A model can produce convincing claims about a protocol's safety, an AI product's reliability or a fintech service's advantages without knowing whether the company can substantiate them. Someone with the relevant knowledge still needs to check the claims before they are published.

Use AI to prepare

Gather notes, organize information, explore possible explanations and make first drafts that humans can inspect.

Use evidence to choose

Look at customer questions, product use, sales objections and campaign results before deciding what deserves attention.

Keep someone accountable

Name the person who approves the claim, the audience, the budget and the final published work.

Measure whether the decision helped

Suppose the DeFi app decides to replace five generic awareness posts with one explanation of the deposit process. The useful measure isn't that the article was delivered quickly. It's whether people who read it understand the product better and complete the next step more often. The team should also check whether any improvement was caused by a product change or a different audience, not assume the article deserves all the credit.

For a company selling infrastructure to businesses, the relevant measure may be fewer confused sales calls or more conversations with the right buyers. For a developer product, it may be successful integrations. The measures should follow the commercial problem.

More AI-assisted work can be good. More unnecessary work is still unnecessary. A team that knows when not to publish has an advantage over one that treats every draft as an asset.

lowob takeaways

  • Start with the problem, not the prompt. Know whom you're trying to help and what is currently stopping them.
  • Let AI speed up work you can evaluate. Research summaries and drafts are useful when someone can verify the result.
  • Keep consequential decisions with an accountable person. Product claims, audience priorities and budget choices need real context and ownership.
  • Judge the work by what changed. Published assets are evidence of activity; customer understanding and valuable actions tell you more about effectiveness.

Sources and notes

Ahrefs: 69% of Marketers Are Publishing More AI Content Than Last Year (30 September 2026). Survey of 301 marketers about AI use in content creation. Findings are descriptive, not proof of marketing performance.

The DeFi example is illustrative, not a real or lowob client result. The editorial framework and recommendations reflect lowob's interpretation of how marketing decisions should be made.
